authorities.name: Abu Dhabi Department of Energy
authorities.role: Regulates power and water in Abu Dhabi and licenses electricity generation. It issues self-supply generation licences for on-site plants above 5 MWp. In January 2026 it said it is designing a dedicated electricity tariff for data centres, and no rates had been published by October 2026.

authorities.name: Emirates Water and Electricity Company (EWEC)
authorities.role: Abu Dhabi's single buyer of power. It plans and contracts the generation that a large campus such as Stargate UAE needs, and it may add gas turbines such as Taweelah C. Corporate and virtual power purchase agreements are generally not allowed, so large sites rely on EWEC supply or their own plants.

authorities.name: Abu Dhabi National Energy Company (TAQA)
authorities.role: Owns the Abu Dhabi transmission and distribution networks through its subsidiaries TRANSCO, ADDC and AADC. A site needs a connection agreement with these operators and pays the ADDC business tariff. TAQA's CEO said in 2025 that investment to power Abu Dhabi's data centre industry will exceed AED 37 billion.

authorities.name: Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA)
authorities.role: The only power and water utility in Dubai. It connects sites and charges industrial users AED 0.380 per kWh above 10,000 kWh a month, plus a monthly fuel surcharge of AED 0.060 per kWh for October 2026. Its subsidiary Moro Hub also builds and runs solar-powered data centres.

authorities.name: Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure (MoEI)
match: National Team for Reviewing the Impact of Data Centers on Energy Sector
authorities.role: Leads a national team, formed in February 2025, that reviews how data centres affect energy demand. The team will list and classify every data centre in the country and map their locations to plan infrastructure. Its main task is a federal policy to regulate data centre operations, which had not been published by October 2026.

authorities.name: Abu Dhabi Investment Office (ADIO)
authorities.role: Gives long-term leases over government land through its Musataha programme. Khazna used it in May 2024 for a 30 MW data centre in Mafraq. ADIO said it had signed 132 such agreements since October 2021.

authorities.name: Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (DIEZ)
authorities.role: Runs the Dubai Silicon Oasis, Dubai Airport Freezone and Dubai CommerCity free zones and licenses firms in them. In May 2026 it formed a joint venture with Volt UAE for a data centre campus in Dubai Silicon Oasis. DIEZ provides the land and base infrastructure, and Volt builds, finances and operates the site.

authorities.name: Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority (TDRA)
match: Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority
authorities.role: Licenses the telecom carriers that connect data centres. On 9 August 2026 it renewed the e& and du licences to 2046 and added duties on network resilience, backup capacity and international connectivity. It also sits on the federal data centre energy team.

authorities.name: Artificial Intelligence and Data Authority
match: UAE Artificial Intelligence and Data Authority
authorities.role: A federal body created on 14 June 2026 that reports to the Cabinet. It merged the UAE Data Office, the digital government arm of TDRA and the AI office. It sets national data standards and proposes data laws, including the delayed rules under the personal data law.

authorities.name: UAE Cyber Security Council
authorities.role: Issued the National Cloud Security Policy in February 2023 and certifies clouds that host government workloads. In May 2026 du's National Hypercloud became the first sovereign cloud certified under it, for all government workloads except Secret and Top Secret.

AE.authorities_note: Power is regulated emirate by emirate, so a site in Abu Dhabi deals with the Department of Energy, EWEC and TAQA and a site in Dubai deals with DEWA. US chip export licences are issued by the US Bureau of Industry and Security, and no UAE body administers them.
authorities_also: The UAE Ministry of Finance sets federal corporate tax at 9% above AED 375,000 and 0% on qualifying income for free zone companies that meet the conditions.
The DIFC Commissioner of Data Protection and the ADGM Office of Data Protection apply separate data protection laws inside the two financial free zones in place of the federal law.
The UAE Ministry of Health and Prevention enforces Federal Law No. 2 of 2019, which bars storing or processing health data outside the UAE unless a health authority allows an exception.

SA.summary: Saudi Arabia requires data centre operators to register with the telecom and technology regulator CST since 1 January 2024, and cloud providers need a CST class that decides which data they may host. Licensed cloud computing gets a flat power tariff of 18 halalas per kWh, and government data must stay in the Kingdom. Advanced US chips arrive only through case by case licences such as Humain's November 2025 approval, because Saudi Arabia has no A:5 status.

approvals.title: CST registration for data centre operators
approvals.text: Data centre service providers that rent out space, power and cooling must register with the Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST). Its Data Centre Services Regulations took effect on 1 January 2024.

sources.title: CST Announces 'Data Center Services Regulations' Document Has Entered into Force
New Data Center Services Regulations come into force in Saudi Arabia

approvals.title: New facilities must be carrier neutral
approvals.text: New registered data centres must be Tier II or Tier III and carrier neutral, meaning any telecom network may connect. Tier I registration is limited to existing sites. A registration lasts three years and requires an energy management and sustainability plan.

sources.title: New Data Center Services Regulations come into force in Saudi Arabia

approvals.title: Cloud providers need a CST class
approvals.text: Cloud service providers must register with CST and receive Class A, B or C. The class sets which data classifications and sectors a provider may serve. Oracle reported in December 2023 that Class C requires hosting in a Tier 3 or higher data centre.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia Cloud Compliance Part 1: Data Residency and Contractual Expectations
OCI achieves CST Class C in Saudi Arabia, demonstrating NCA ECC and CCC compliance

approvals.title: Municipal licence rules for data centres
approvals.text: The Ministry of Municipalities and Housing set unified rules for standalone commercial data centres inside and outside city limits. Operators need Civil Defense approval, a commercial registration covering the activity and approval from the sector supervisor. Buildings must follow the Saudi Building Code.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia approves municipal requirements for commercial data centers
Saudi Arabia adopts municipal regulations for commercial data centers

approvals.title: Draft Global AI Hub Law
approvals.text: CST published a draft law in April 2025 for hubs that host foreign data. It proposes private hubs for foreign governments with diplomatic protections, plus extended and virtual hubs where a foreign country's law can govern the data. Public comment closed on 14 May 2025.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia offers data sovereignty to foreign countries with ‘AI hub’ law
Global AI Hub Law
sources.publisher: Istitlaa (National Competitiveness Center public consultation platform)

approvals.title: US chip licence for Humain only
approvals.text: On 19 November 2025 the US Commerce Department authorised Humain to buy about 35,000 Nvidia GB300 chips. The approval is a case by case licence with security and reporting conditions monitored by the Bureau of Industry and Security. Saudi Arabia has no country level US framework for advanced chips.
approvals.authority: US Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security

sources.title: Statement on UAE and Saudi Chip Exports

approvals.title: NEOM leases Oxagon land for AI campus
approvals.text: NEOM signed an agreement with DataVolt on 10 February 2025 for a 1.5 GW AI data centre campus in Oxagon. Oxagon leases the land and gives infrastructure support. DataVolt's first US$5 billion funds phase one. DataVolt and HUMAIN broke ground on the first 100 MW in August 2026 and expect power in 2028.

sources.title: DataVolt signs agreement with NEOM
DataVolt and HUMAIN break ground on first AI data center in NEOM

power.title: Special power tariff for cloud computing
power.text: The Cabinet approved a power tariff of 0.18 riyals per kilowatt hour (kWh) for cloud computing companies licensed by the telecom regulator in March 2021. The Saudi Electricity Company tariff table still lists Cloud Computing at a flat 18 halalas per kWh. A halala is one hundredth of a riyal.
power.authority: Council of Ministers, Ministry of Energy

sources.title: New power tariff to stimulate investments in cloud computing field: energy minister
Consumption Tariffs

power.title: Standard business tariff brackets
power.text: Commercial users pay 22 halalas per kWh for the first 6,000 kWh a month and 32 halalas above that. Industrial users pay a flat 20 halalas per kWh. Government users pay 32 halalas per kWh.
power.authority: Saudi Electricity Regulatory Authority (SERA), Saudi Electricity Company

sources.title: Consumption Tariffs

power.title: Heavy consumption tariff by grid connection
power.text: Eligible industrial, commercial and farm users where power is 20 percent or more of operating cost pay 18 halalas per kWh on the distribution network and 12 on the transmission network. Users where power is 10 to 19.9 percent of cost pay 24 and 18. The rate cannot exceed the user's normal category rate.

sources.title: Consumption Tariffs
SEC Calls on Establishments to Apply for the Intensive Electricity Consumption Tariff

power.title: Surcharge for non eligible heavy users
power.text: From 28 May 2025 industrial, commercial and farm users that do not qualify for the heavy consumption tariff pay an extra 2 halalas per kWh. The Saudi Electricity Company said this rate will be updated from time to time.
power.authority: Saudi Electricity Company, Saudi Electricity Regulatory Authority (SERA)

sources.title: SEC Calls on Establishments to Apply for the Intensive Electricity Consumption Tariff

power.title: Large consumers can negotiate prices
power.text: The Electricity Law defines a Large Consumer as one whose use exceeds a limit set by the regulator. Article 12 lets a licensed power company agree prices with a Large Consumer that differ from the approved tariff.

sources.title: Electricity Law

incentives.title: Cloud Computing Special Economic Zone
incentives.text: The Crown Prince launched a Cloud Computing Special Economic Zone on 13 April 2023. CST regulates it with the Economic Cities and Special Zones Authority. It targets cloud providers and firms in AI and other advanced technology.
incentives.authority: Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST), Economic Cities and Special Zones Authority

sources.title: To promote Saudi Arabia’s position as a global investment hub H.R.H. the Crown Prince launches the Cloud Computing Special Economic Zone

incentives.title: Zone rules took effect April 2026
incentives.text: The Cabinet approved regulatory frameworks for four zones including the Cloud Computing zone in January 2026. They took effect on 16 April 2026. Cloud zone companies may build data centres anywhere in the Kingdom if their headquarters is in Riyadh.
incentives.authority: Council of Ministers, Economic Cities and Special Zones Authority

sources.title: Saudi Arabia publishes regulatory framework for 4 SEZs
Saudi Arabia publishes regulatory frameworks governing four of its special economic zones

incentives.title: Advertised 5 percent zone tax
incentives.text: At launch the zones were promoted with 5 percent corporate income tax for up to 20 years, zero withholding tax on profits sent abroad and zero customs duty on capital equipment. The 2026 zone frameworks refer back to the Tax Law and its incentives without stating a flat rate.
incentives.authority: Economic Cities and Special Zones Authority

sources.title: Saudi Arabia - Launches four special economic zones (SEZ)
Saudi Arabia publishes regulatory frameworks governing four of its special economic zones

incentives.title: Riyadh logistics zone offers exemptions
incentives.text: The Special Integrated Logistics Zone at King Khalid International Airport opened in October 2022 with exemptions from certain taxes and labour rules. Its launch named technology, communications, aviation and pharmaceuticals as focus industries. Data centres were not named.
incentives.authority: Ministry of Transport and Logistic Services

sources.title: Transport minister launches Kingdom’s first Special Integrated Logistics Zone, Apple first investor

incentives.title: MODON leases land for data centres
incentives.text: The industrial cities authority MODON signed a land lease agreement with DataVolt in February 2025 for a 55,000 square metre data centre site. The site is in the First Technology Park in east Riyadh.
incentives.authority: Saudi Authority for Industrial Cities and Technology Zones (MODON)

sources.title: DataVolt Signs an Agreement with the Saudi Authority for Industrial Cities and Technology Zones to Build a Data Center Facility in Riyadh

data.title: Personal data law fully enforced
data.text: The Personal Data Protection Law took effect on 14 September 2023 with a one year grace period. Full compliance became mandatory on 14 September 2024. It also covers foreign firms that process data of Saudi residents.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia Personal Data Protection Law: Transition Period Ends September 14

data.title: Rules for sending data abroad
data.text: An amended regulation on transferring personal data outside the Kingdom took effect on 14 September 2024. Firms may rely on standard contract clauses, binding group rules or an accreditation certificate. A risk assessment is required in some cases including sensitive data.

sources.title: New SDAIA rules and guidelines published as KSA’s personal data protection framework is now enforceable
Saudi Arabia Personal Data Protection Law: Transition Period Ends September 14

data.title: Government data stays in the Kingdom
data.text: Government agency data must remain inside Saudi Arabia with only narrow exceptions set by law. Offshore hosting of financial institution data needs prior approval from the Saudi Central Bank.
data.authority: Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST), Saudi Central Bank

sources.title: Saudi Arabia Cloud Compliance Part 1: Data Residency and Contractual Expectations

data.title: NCA cloud cybersecurity controls
data.text: The National Cybersecurity Authority sets Cloud Cybersecurity Controls in a second edition dated 2024 for cloud providers and their customers. The controls extend its Essential Cybersecurity Controls and were updated to reflect data localisation requirements. The NCA page was last updated on 24 June 2026.

sources.title: Cloud Cybersecurity Controls

data.title: Data controllers must register
data.text: Public bodies, firms whose main activity is processing personal data and firms handling sensitive data must register on the National Data Governance Platform.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia Personal Data Protection Law: Transition Period Ends September 14

water.title: Cooling must meet set standards
water.text: The 2026 municipal rules require commercial data centres to meet local and international standards for cooling systems, fire protection, power and backup. No water use limit for data centres was found.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia adopts municipal regulations for commercial data centers

water.title: Business water tariff set in 2015
water.text: From 16 December 2015 government bodies and large businesses paid 9 riyals per cubic metre for water and sanitation and 6 riyals for water only. No newer official rate for data centres was confirmed.
water.authority: Ministry of Environment, Water and Agriculture

sources.title: Saudi Arabia raises business water tariff by 50%

watching.title: Saudi Arabia lacks A:5 chip status
watching.text: On 14 July 2026 the US moved the UAE into Country Group A:5, which lets named users buy advanced chips without a licence. Saudi Arabia received no such rule. Fortune reported on 9 September 2026 that the Kingdom still lacks the designation.
watching.authority: US Bureau of Industry and Security

sources.publisher: Federal Register (US Bureau of Industry and Security)

watching.title: Global AI Hub Law still pending
watching.text: No final approval of the Global AI Hub Law was found after public comment closed on 14 May 2025. The consultation text says the law would take effect 60 days after publication in the official gazette.

sources.title: Global AI Hub Law
sources.publisher: Istitlaa (National Competitiveness Center public consultation platform)

watching.title: Push for private AI data centre money
watching.text: The investment and communications ministries held a workshop on 10 June 2026 with banks, investors, Humain and the AI Enablement Office. It discussed ways to raise private sector funding for AI data centres.
watching.authority: Ministry of Investment (MISA), Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)

sources.title: Investment and communications ministries explore private investment opportunities in AI data centers

watching.title: Humain seeks outside investors
watching.text: Fortune reported on 9 September 2026 that Humain is seeking outside investment as the state limits spending. An expert quoted linked this to a possible US arrangement similar to the one G42 obtained.

sources.title: Saudi's Humain turns to outside investment as the kingdom reins in fiscal spending

watching.title: Surcharge rate under periodic review
watching.text: The Saudi Electricity Company said the surcharge on users outside the heavy consumption tariff will be updated periodically. Data centre operators should watch for revised rates.

sources.title: SEC Calls on Establishments to Apply for the Intensive Electricity Consumption Tariff

authorities.name: Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST)
authorities.role: Registers data centre service providers under its Data Centre Services Regulations, in force since 1 January 2024. New sites must be Tier II or Tier III and carrier neutral, and a registration lasts three years. CST also classes cloud providers, co-regulates the Cloud Computing Special Economic Zone, and drafted the Global AI Hub Law in April 2025, which was still not final by October 2026.

authorities.name: Ministry of Municipalities and Housing
authorities.role: Issues the municipal licence for a standalone commercial data centre inside or outside city limits under rules set in April 2026. An operator needs Civil Defense approval, a commercial registration that covers the activity and approval from the sector supervisor. Buildings must follow the Saudi Building Code and meet cooling, fire, power and backup standards.

authorities.name: Saudi Energy Company (formerly Saudi Electricity Company)
authorities.role: The national utility that connects and supplies data centres through its grid arm National Grid SA. Shareholders approved the rename from Saudi Electricity Company on 25 February 2026. On 2 September 2026 National Grid SA signed a deal to supply power to a HUMAIN AI data centre in Riyadh, and its project subsidiary signed a framework deal with center3.

authorities.name: Saudi Electricity Regulatory Authority (SERA)
authorities.role: Sets the framework for grid connection, capacity allocation, tariffs and reliability with the Ministry of Energy. It approved the heavy consumption tariff from 28 May 2025, which can fall to 12 halalas per kWh on the transmission network. Under the Electricity Law it sets the limit above which a large consumer may negotiate its own price.

authorities.name: Ministry of Energy
match: Council of Ministers, Ministry of Energy
authorities.role: Sets energy policy and oversees renewable power procurement. In March 2021 the Cabinet approved a cloud computing tariff of 0.18 riyals per kWh for companies licensed by the telecom regulator, which the energy minister announced.

authorities.name: Saudi Data and AI Authority (SDAIA)
match: Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority
authorities.role: Enforces the Personal Data Protection Law and its rules on sending data abroad, fully in force since 14 September 2024. It also builds government capacity. On 5 January 2026 it laid the foundation stone for Hexagon, a 480 MW Tier IV government data centre in Riyadh.

authorities.name: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
match: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
Ministry of Communications and Information Technology
authorities.role: Leads the national data centre strategy unveiled in June 2025 with SDAIA, which targets up to 1.5 GW of capacity by 2030. In June 2026 it held a workshop with the Ministry of Investment and banks on private funding for AI data centres.

authorities.name: Ministry of Investment (MISA)
authorities.role: Under the Investment Law, a foreign investor must register with MISA before investing, in place of the old licence. Activities on the restricted list need MISA approval. MISA also works with MCIT to bring private money into AI data centres.

authorities.name: Economic Cities and Special Zones Authority (ECZA)
match: Economic Cities and Special Zones Authority
authorities.role: Oversees the special economic zones, including the Cloud Computing zone it regulates with CST. The zone rules approved in January 2026 took effect on 16 April 2026. Cloud zone companies may build data centres anywhere in the Kingdom if their headquarters is in Riyadh.

authorities.name: Saudi Authority for Industrial Cities and Technology Zones (MODON)
match: Saudi Authority for Industrial Cities and Technology Zones (MODON)
authorities.role: Leases land in industrial cities and technology zones. In February 2025 it signed a lease with DataVolt for a 55,000 square metre data centre site in the First Technology Park in east Riyadh.

authorities.name: NEOM
authorities.role: Leases land and provides infrastructure in its Oxagon industrial city for a planned 1.5 GW AI campus. DataVolt and HUMAIN broke ground on the first 100 MW there in August 2026, with power expected in 2028.

authorities.name: National Cybersecurity Authority (NCA)
authorities.role: Sets the Cloud Cybersecurity Controls that cloud providers and their customers must meet, now in a 2024 second edition. The controls build on its Essential Cybersecurity Controls and reflect data localisation rules.

SA.authorities_note: US chip export licences for Saudi buyers are issued case by case by the US Bureau of Industry and Security, and no Saudi body administers them.
authorities_also: The Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) is the single buyer that signs power purchase agreements for new renewable and storage capacity under Ministry of Energy oversight.
The Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) must approve in advance any offshore hosting of a financial institution's data.

QA.summary: Qatar regulates cloud and data centre activity through a 2022 Cloud Policy Framework, CRA cloud regulations, national cyber security policies and a 2016 personal data law. We found no dedicated data centre licence. Large AI builds, such as the US$20 billion Qai and Brookfield venture, also need US export licences for advanced chips.

approvals.title: Cabinet approved national Cloud Policy Framework
approvals.text: The Cabinet approved Qatar's Cloud Policy Framework on 1 June 2022. The Communications Regulatory Authority (CRA) published it to set trusted access principles and attract data centre and cloud investment.

sources.title: CRA publishes Cloud Policy Framework
CRA Publishes the Cloud Policy Framework

approvals.title: CRA rules on cloud data portability
approvals.text: The CRA issued a regulation on cloud data interoperability and data portability on 25 November 2024. Cloud service providers in Qatar must build data portability into their services and give government customers application programming interfaces (APIs) so their systems can work together.

sources.title: Regulation for Cloud Data Interoperability and Data Portability

approvals.title: US licence needed for advanced AI chips
approvals.text: Qatar is in US export control Country Group D:4. Since an October 2023 rule, exports of advanced AI chips to Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 need a US licence.
approvals.authority: US Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security

sources.title: Implementation of Additional Export Controls: Certain Advanced Computing Items; Supercomputer and Semiconductor End Use; Updates and Corrections
Supplement No. 1 to Part 740, Country Groups

power.title: Kahramaa tiered electricity tariff from 2015
power.text: Gulf Times reported that Kahramaa's revised electricity tariff from September 2015 rose from QR0.08 to QR0.10 per kWh across three usage tiers. The report said the tiers applied to all establishments, including commercial and industrial users. We could not confirm the current rate on Kahramaa's own website.
power.authority: Kahramaa (Qatar General Electricity and Water Corporation)

sources.title: Kahramaa hikes water, electricity tariffs

power.title: Renewable share to rise by 2030
power.text: Kahramaa told the Shura Council in June 2026 that it plans to raise the share of renewables in the energy mix by 2030. Solar photovoltaic power is the focus of this plan.

sources.title: Shura Council reviews Kahramaa energy plans

incentives.title: Free zone tax exemption lasts 20 years
incentives.text: Qatar Free Zones offers a 20 year corporate tax exemption and zero customs duties on imports. It also allows 100% foreign ownership and full repatriation of capital.

sources.title: Business Friendly

incentives.title: Invest Qatar US$1 billion incentive programme
incentives.text: Invest Qatar launched a US$1 billion incentive programme on 21 May 2025. Its technology package covers cloud computing, AI and cybersecurity. It pays up to 40% of eligible local costs over five years, such as construction and equipment. Projects must invest at least QAR 25 million over five years and meet job targets.

sources.title: Invest Qatar Unveils USD1 Billion Incentives Program to Boost Foreign, Local Investments

data.title: Personal data law allows cross border flows
data.text: Article 15 of Law No. 13 of 2016 bars controllers from limiting cross border data flows. The exception is where the processing breaches the law or may seriously harm the data or the individual's privacy.

sources.title: Law No.13 of 2016 - Personal Data Privacy Protection

data.title: Data law fines reach QR5 million
data.text: Breaches of certain articles of the 2016 personal data law carry fines of up to QR5 million. These include the rules on sensitive personal data, such as health, religion and ethnic origin.

sources.title: Law No.13 of 2016 - Personal Data Privacy Protection

data.title: Government cloud must stay in GCC
data.text: The national Cloud Security Policy says government agencies shall not use a cloud provider outside Qatar and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) unless the service meets Qatari privacy law and data classification rules.

sources.title: Cloud Security Policy Version: 1.3

data.title: Central bank rules govern financial cloud use
data.text: Qatar Central Bank (QCB) issued cloud computing regulations for financial institutions and fintech firms in April 2024. They cover cloud governance, the cloud lifecycle and operational security controls.

sources.title: QCB Issues Cloud Computing Regulations
QCB issues ‘Cloud Computing’ regulations

data.title: NCSA promotes national data classification policy
data.text: In May 2026 the NCSA set out the stages of its Data Classification Policy. Organisations must keep a data inventory, label data by value and apply technical and administrative safeguards such as encryption.

sources.title: NCSA outlines data classification policy pillars to strengthen digital security

water.title: Kahramaa tiered water tariff from 2015
water.text: Gulf Times reported that Kahramaa's water tariff from September 2015 rose from QR4.40 to QR7.40 per cubic metre across usage tiers. We could not confirm whether these rates still apply.

sources.title: Kahramaa hikes water, electricity tariffs

watching.title: Qai and Brookfield form AI venture
watching.text: Qai, an AI company owned by the Qatar Investment Authority, formed a US$20 billion AI infrastructure joint venture with Brookfield in December 2025. It will build in Qatar and selected overseas markets.

sources.title: Qatar launches AI infrastructure investment venture following AI company launch

watching.title: Syntys buys Q Data free zone sites
watching.text: Ooredoo's data centre arm Syntys bought Q Data QFZ from the Qatar Free Zones venture arm in January 2026. The deal took Syntys to 26MW of live IT capacity in Qatar.

sources.title: Ooredoo's Syntys acquires two data centers in Qatar

watching.title: Minister aims to triple capacity
watching.text: The Minister of Communications and Information Technology said in May 2024 that Qatar aims to triple its data centre capacity in five to six years. He also wants more hyperscalers, the largest cloud providers, to set up in Qatar.
watching.authority: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)

sources.title: Data centre capacity to grow three times in five to six years

watching.title: Shura members question commercial tariffs
watching.text: Shura Council members raised concerns about electricity and water tariffs for commercial users during a June 2026 review of Kahramaa. No tariff change was announced.

sources.title: Shura Council reviews Kahramaa energy plans

Current Kahramaa commercial and industrial tariffs published on km.qa, or any data centre specific power tariff.
Data centre specific incentives from the Investment Promotion Agency Qatar.
Data localisation rules in the QCB cloud regulation, since the full text could not be retrieved.
QFC data protection regulations and any 2026 amendment to Law No. 13 of 2016.

Water use, cooling or treated sewage effluent rules specific to data centres.

authorities.name: Communications Regulatory Authority (CRA)
authorities.role: Regulates telecom and cloud services. It published the national Cloud Policy Framework that the Cabinet approved in June 2022. On 25 November 2024 it issued a regulation that requires cloud providers to build in data portability and give government customers APIs.

authorities.name: Qatar General Electricity and Water Corporation (Kahramaa)
match: Kahramaa (Qatar General Electricity and Water Corporation)
authorities.role: The only electricity and water utility, so every site needs its connection. Its 2015 tariff runs from QR0.08 to QR0.10 per kWh. In June 2026 it told the Shura Council it plans more solar power by 2030, and members questioned commercial tariffs.

authorities.name: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
match: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
Ministry of Communications and Information Technology
authorities.role: Sets digital policy under the Digital Agenda 2030. The minister said in May 2024 that Qatar aims to triple data centre capacity in five to six years and attract more hyperscalers.

authorities.name: National Cyber Security Agency (NCSA)
authorities.role: Enforces the 2016 personal data law and sets the national Cloud Security Policy. Under that policy, government agencies may use providers outside Qatar and the GCC only if Qatari privacy and classification rules are met. In May 2026 it set out the stages of its Data Classification Policy.

authorities.name: Qatar Free Zones Authority (QFZ)
authorities.role: Licenses firms in the Ras Bufontas and Umm Alhoul free zones and offers a 20-year corporate tax exemption with 100% foreign ownership. In January 2026 its venture arm sold the Q Data QFZ data centres to Ooredoo's Syntys.

authorities.name: Invest Qatar (Investment Promotion Agency Qatar)
authorities.role: Runs a US$1 billion incentive programme whose technology package covers cloud computing, AI and cybersecurity. It covers up to 40% of eligible local investment costs over five years for projects of at least QAR 25 million that create at least five skilled jobs. The next application window had not been announced.

authorities.name: Qatar Central Bank (QCB)
authorities.role: Sets cloud rules for banks and fintech firms, issued in April 2024. They cover cloud governance, the cloud lifecycle and security controls, which decides whether financial workloads can move into a data centre.

QA.authorities_note: US chip export licences for Qatar are issued by the US Bureau of Industry and Security, and no Qatari body administers them.
authorities_also: The Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) owns Qai, which formed a US$20 billion AI infrastructure joint venture with Brookfield in December 2025 to build in Qatar and abroad.

BH.summary: Bahrain says it is the only country with a Data Embassy law, which lets foreign customers keep data stored in Bahrain under their home country's law. Commercial and other unsubsidised users have paid up to 32 fils per kWh since January 2026, about US$0.085. Personal data can leave Bahrain without approval only to countries on an official adequacy list.

approvals.title: Data Embassy law covers foreign data
approvals.text: Legislative Decree No. 56 of 2018 lets foreign customers store data in Bahrain data centres under the law of their home country. In January 2026 the finance minister said Bahrain remained the only country with such a law.

sources.title: Bahrain still the only country with a ‘Data Embassy’ law in an AI-driven age, finance minister says

approvals.title: Government follows Cloud First policy
approvals.text: Bahrain's government adopted a Cloud First policy in 2017 to move public IT spending toward cloud services. By January 2022 over 70% of systems from 72 government entities had moved to the cloud.

sources.title: Bahrain government successfully adopts Cloud First Policy

approvals.text: Bahrain is in US export control Country Group D:4. Since an October 2023 rule, exports of advanced AI chips to Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 need a US licence.

power.text: The Cabinet raised the electricity tariff for unsubsidised users, including commercial users, from 29 fils to 32 fils per kWh from January 2026.

power.title: Power costs 33.1 fils to produce
power.text: The minister responsible for electricity said in March 2026 that producing one kWh costs 33.1 fils. He said industrial users pay 25 fils, with the state covering the 8.1 fils gap.

incentives.title: Golden Licence fast tracks large projects
incentives.text: Bahrain's Golden Licence, launched in April 2023, gives large investment projects priority processing and faster land allocation. Gulf Business reported that data centres were among the sectors it had supported by March 2024.

data.title: Free transfers only to adequate countries
data.text: Article 12 of the Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 30 of 2018) allows transfers abroad to places with adequate protection. Order No. 42 of 2022 lists these countries, and transfers elsewhere need case by case approval from the data protection authority.

sources.title: Ministry of Justice, Islamic Affairs and Waqf Order No. (42) of 2022

data.title: Banks need approval for cloud outsourcing
data.text: Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB) rules require licensees to get the CBB's prior written approval before entering any material cloud outsourcing arrangement. The rules also require encryption of sensitive data at rest and in transit.

water.title: Commercial water costs 775 fils
water.text: EWA charges non-domestic and commercial users 775 fils per cubic metre of water. The rate rose from 750 fils in January 2026.

watching.text: Batelco signed a memorandum with Qareeb Data Centres in November 2024 for a site in southern Bahrain. The 140,000 square metre facility is planned to run fully on solar power.

watching.title: SeaMeWe-6 cable expected in 2026
watching.text: Bahrain is connecting to the SeaMeWe-6 subsea cable, which runs from Singapore to France. It was expected to launch in early 2026.

authorities.name: Electricity and Water Authority (EWA)
authorities.role: The only power and water utility, so it connects and supplies every site. It charges commercial users 32 fils per kWh above 5,000 units and 775 fils per cubic metre of water from January 2026. The minister said in March 2026 that a kWh costs 33.1 fils to produce.

authorities.name: Council of Ministers
authorities.role: Designates the data centres and foreign states covered by the Data Embassy law, Legislative Decree No. 56 of 2018, by a regulation in the official gazette. Under that law a foreign customer's data falls under the law of its home country. The Cabinet also raised the unsubsidised power tariff from 29 to 32 fils per kWh from January 2026.

authorities.name: Bahrain Economic Development Board (EDB)
authorities.role: Brings in data centre investors and runs the Golden Licence, launched in April 2023. The licence gives large projects priority processing and faster land allocation, and data centres were among the sectors it had supported by March 2024.

authorities.name: Information and eGovernment Authority (iGA)
authorities.role: Runs the government's Cloud First policy, adopted in 2017, which moves public IT spending to cloud services. By January 2022 over 70% of systems from 72 government entities had moved to the cloud.

authorities.name: Personal Data Protection Authority
authorities.role: Enforces the 2018 personal data law. Data may go freely only to the countries listed in Order No. 42 of 2022. Transfers elsewhere need its case by case approval.

authorities.name: Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB)
authorities.role: Its licensees need its prior written approval before any material cloud outsourcing. The rules also require encryption of sensitive data at rest and in transit.

BH.authorities_note: US chip export licences for Bahrain are issued by the US Bureau of Industry and Security, and no Bahraini body administers them.
authorities_also: The Attorney General must be told in writing when a cloud provider receives a foreign court order under the Data Embassy law, and can order it enforced.
